sentences.t: The city passed a moratorium, then repealed the ordinance that would have allowed the project, and the developer sued.

Thor Equities, of New York, proposes the Urbana Technology Hub, a single storey data center of about 460,000 square feet near the junction of Ohio 55 and US 68 at Urbana, in Champaign County, close to the Rittal plant.
The company says it has spent more than $19 million on the development and projects $3 million a year in tax revenue.

Urbana City Council passed a twelve month moratorium on data center construction in March 2026, after residents gathered more than 4,000 signatures against data centers in Champaign County and more than thirty people spoke against the project at the meeting.
On June 16, 2026 the council went further and voted to repeal Ordinance 4621-25, banning data centers from the city.

Three days later, on June 19, Thor Equities filed a federal lawsuit against the city, its council and its board of zoning appeals, alleging Urbana broke state and local law by changing the rules after the company had applied.

The company's complaint says: "The City's actions have caused lost investment, delayed project timelines, impaired business relationships, and deprived the local community of jobs, tax revenue, and the benefits of planned infrastructure improvements."
Its statement was softer: "Thor looks forward to resolving this matter fairly so it can continue being a strong partner for Urbana and help build a brighter future for the city."
Thor Equities is the same company whose Augusta Township proposal in Michigan was overturned by referendum in August 2026, 89.5 percent against.
Urbana Township adopted its own moratorium on March 3, 2026, and three more measures sit within reach: Dayton's ban from June 25, 2026 and two Springfield moratoriums from June and July.
There is no other data center site on record anywhere in Champaign County, and none within 40 kilometres.
The nearest generators are all solar: 180, 144, 196 and 325 megawatt farms between 26 and 46 kilometres away.

unconfirmed: No resident or council member is quoted: the report read here carries none by name, and the WOSU, WDTN and Springfield News-Sun accounts were found only in search summaries, as was the 4,000 signature petition. The 100 megawatt figure in our record is not confirmed by anything read, and the 48 acres is not stated either; the reporting gives building size rather than site size. What the repealed Ordinance 4621-25 actually did, and whether the moratorium or the repeal is the subject of the suit, are not fully explained in it. A recall effort in Urbana is referred to in one headline that was not opened. The outcome of the federal case is unknown.

sentences.t: The township banned them before anyone applied.

On December 17, 2025 Waterville Township trustees, in Lucas County, voted unanimously for a twelve month moratorium on data centers, saying they would use the year to look into what such buildings do, and became the second place in the Toledo region to do it.
The entry stands as proposed at an early stage, with no address beyond the township, no acreage, no capacity, no cost and no developer, at medium confidence, and describes it as a land advertisement.
Its only source is a Toledo Blade report from April 23, 2026 headlined that a company is interested in Waterville Township; that page returned only its navigation.

What the searches did find is that in August 2026 Lucas County leaders declared a 150 acre site near the junction of Waterville Neapolis and Waterville Monclova Roads ready for development, and said specifically that it would not be a data center.
Whether that is the same land this entry refers to is not established.
The region has moved as a bloc.

Seven measures sit within reach on record: Waterville Township from December 18, 2025, Maumee and Monclova in February 2026, Lake Township and Frenchtown Township in March, Erie Township on March 16 and Findlay on April 22.
Ohio as a whole had more than 125 active data center moratoriums by September 2026.
The Monclova entry on record, also without a named developer or site, is six kilometres away, Meta's operating Bowling Green campus 16, and the proposed 500 megawatt Oregon project 33.
The nearest generators are the 707 megawatt Troy Energy plant 24 kilometres off and the 849 megawatt Oregon Clean Energy Center at 32.

unconfirmed: The Blade page returned only site furniture and no article text, and the Toledo Free Press piece headlined that a hyperscale data center is eyed for Waterville Township was not fetched, so no source url is listed and each sentence is attributed to our record's source list. No company, site, acreage or capacity has been established. No resident or trustee is quoted. This entry records interest rather than a proposal, which our record's "proposed (early)" status fairly reflects.

sentences.t: The buyer walked away, and then the city stopped taking applications anyway.

After the city was told a letter of intent had expired between a private landowner and a prospective buyer for 52 acres of east Broken Arrow, in Wagoner County, the city manager Michael Spurgeon recommended a moratorium on data centers.

On June 15, 2026 the city council approved a six month pause, freezing new rezoning requests, building permits and other approvals for data centers with immediate effect, to run until December 31, 2026.

The council said staff would use the time to look at electricity use and what it would do to utility rates for other customers, water demand, noise, traffic, the state tax exemptions that apply to data centers, and the load on public infrastructure.
The project is recorded as proposed with no acreage, no capacity, no cost and no developer, at medium confidence, and pushback marked unknown.
The acreage the record omits is 52, and the buyer was never named.
Broken Arrow sits inside one of the densest clusters of data center activity in Oklahoma.

Nine other recorded sites lie within 36 kilometres: a TierPoint building 11 kilometres away, a Compass site at 12, Project Anthem under construction at 12, the cancelled Project Atlas at 20, Meta's Tulsa campus under construction at 26, an operating Cherokee data center at 29, Google's Project Clydesdale under construction at 30, another Google project at 35 and Project Mustang at 36.
The gas is close: the 1,086 megawatt Oneta Energy Center is five kilometres away, the 783 megawatt Green Country plant 18, the 1,070 megawatt Riverside plant 20 and the 330 megawatt Tulsa plant 24.
Tulsa adopted its own moratorium on March 25, 2026, also running to the end of the year.

unconfirmed: The city's own news pages and information page were not fetched, the Data Center Dynamics report in our record is not fetchable, and the News on 6 accounts were found only in search summaries, so no source url is listed and each sentence is attributed to our record's source list. No council member or resident is quoted. Whether the 52 acres in east Broken Arrow is the site our record maps at the Creek Turnpike and Highway 51, and whether any developer has returned since the letter of intent expired, are unknown.

sentences.t: The first phase is going ahead; the second was pulled days after the city stopped taking new applications.

Atmoss LLC is building the Project Anthem data center on 340 acres at Fair Oaks Industrial Park near 11th Street and the Creek Turnpike in east Tulsa, on land the record files under Wagoner County, with construction on phase one due to start in the spring of 2026.

It had also sought zoning changes on about 375 more acres for phase two, moving the land from agricultural to light industrial and changing the city's comprehensive plan designation from neighbourhood to employment.
Tulsa adopted a nine month halt on new data centers on March 25, 2026.
The moratorium exempted both phases of Project Anthem, so Atmoss could have carried on with the rezoning, and chose not to.
The company said it was exploring options and that a phase two remains possible.
The project is recorded as under construction on 340 acres, with no capacity figure, no cost and no developer field filled in, and pushback marked unknown.
No megawatt figure has been published for a campus of this size, which is the number that would tell a neighbour what it means.

Ten other recorded data center sites sit within 38 kilometres, including Google's Project Clydesdale under construction at 21, Meta's Tulsa campus at 23, and Google's operating 368 megawatt Pryor campus at 38.
The 1,086 megawatt Oneta Energy Center is 16 kilometres away, the 1,070 megawatt Riverside plant 26 and the 783 megawatt Green Country plant 26.

The entry gave the address town as Cartoosa, a misspelling of Catoosa, which has been corrected; the Wagoner County placing matches the Fair Oaks park the reporting describes at 11th Street and the Creek Turnpike.

unconfirmed: The Fox23 report in our record returned HTTP 404, the two Data Center Dynamics reports are not fetchable, and the News on 6 and Tulsa World accounts were found only in search summaries, so no source url is listed and each sentence is attributed to our record's source list. No resident, council member or company representative is quoted. The exact date of the phase two withdrawal is not established beyond late March 2026. No megawatt, water or cost figure has been published. Who owns Atmoss LLC is not known.

sentences.t: The council approved it, and residents filed to recall them.

Claremore City Council approved Project Mustang, a multi-phase data center development by Beale Infrastructure in the city's industrial park in Rogers County, with up to three buildings and the first phase targeted for completion in 2028.
Recall and referendum petitions were then filed in Claremore over the decision.
The money is the argument on both sides.

The agreement lets Beale Infrastructure seek a 25 year exemption from ad valorem tax for each phase, while the company says the development would still put more than $250 million into Rogers County schools, municipal services and community programmes over time.
Residents packed the city hall, with supporters and opponents arguing over jobs, taxes and what it would do to the neighbourhoods.
Debbie Cassita, a resident, said she was worried about the effect on the homes nearby and on property values.

The project is recorded as proposed with no acreage, no capacity and no cost, and no developer field filled in, and a petition asking for a permanent ban on AI data centers in Rogers County is on file.
Beale Infrastructure is the same company behind Google's Project Clydesdale at Owasso, 28 kilometres away, and behind Project Atlas at Coweta, which it withdrew.
The generation around Claremore is heavy.
The 1,342 megawatt Northeastern gas plant is 13 kilometres away, the 888 megawatt Chouteau plant 32, the 960 megawatt GREC plant 33 and the 1,086 megawatt Oneta Energy Center 38.
Google's operating 368 megawatt Pryor campus is 27 kilometres off, and seven other recorded sites lie within 36.
Neither Claremore nor Rogers County has a data center moratorium on record; the only measures within reach are Tulsa's and Broken Arrow's, both running to the end of 2026.

unconfirmed: The Data Center Dynamics report in our record is not fetchable, and the KTUL, News on 6 and Fox23 accounts, along with the city's own project plan PDF and FAQ page, were not fetched, so no source url is listed and each sentence is attributed to our record's source list. The date of the council's approval is not established. No acreage, megawatt or water figure has been published. Whether the recall and referendum petitions gathered enough signatures is unknown. Our record's developer field is empty although Beale Infrastructure is named throughout the reporting.

sentences.t: The first question in Luther was where the water would come from.
Beltline Energy presented a data center concept to the Luther Board of Trustees on Thursday, May 29, 2025, for about 400 acres east of an OG&E generating station at Luther, in Oklahoma County.
Mayor Terry Arps said: "Beltline Energy introduced a very basic concept of a data center, without specifics, for the Board to consider."
Jenni White, a former mayor of Luther, put the worry plainly: "I think that concerns a lot of people initially is oh gosh where is this water gonna come from."

She went on to the rest of it: "Then you'd have that on top of a data center, which the batteries can catch fire and it takes forever to put them out. Sucking the electricity ... it's just really an enormous concern."

The resident Saundra Traywick raised what it would do to land: "These industries will target Oklahoma and then they could also purchase land at skyrocketing prices to put in solar and wind," and: "Our landscape is gonna completely change if we don't step in and help us save Oklahoma's farms and ranches."
Behind that is Senate Bill 480, signed this legislative session, which lets certain companies and individuals generate power on their own property without being regulated as public utilities.
Oklahoma City had already adopted one on April 21, Edmond on June 8 and Norman on June 26.
The project is recorded as proposed on 400 acres, with Beltline Energy as developer, no capacity figure and no cost, at medium confidence.
Beltline Energy is the same company behind the three entries at Pacific, Missouri, on record.
The 1,214 megawatt Redbud power plant is one kilometre from the site, the 468 megawatt Horseshoe Lake plant 20 kilometres and the 294 megawatt Spring Creek plant 40.
For all that, the nearest neighbour of the same kind is small and far off: a ten megawatt Cerebras Systems building 32 kilometres away is the only other data center site the record holds within 40.

unconfirmed: No application had been filed at the time of the reporting, and no acreage beyond the approximate 400, no megawatt figure and no water figure have been published since. The presentation was in May 2025, a year before the town's moratorium; the page had given it as June 2025, and whether Beltline Energy came back in between is unknown. The Data Center Dynamics and News 9 accounts in our record were not fetched. Whether the Luther moratorium was extended past December 31, 2026 is unknown.

sentences.t: This one was built to survive an F5.

The data center at 4442 Newcastle Road, on a four acre site near Will Rogers World Airport in Oklahoma City, is about 65,000 square feet with roughly 20,000 square feet of raised floor, and its twelve inch concrete walls, two kinds of concrete with a compressible layer between them, are designed to take winds of up to 310 miles an hour.
Devon Energy built it around 2009 and 2010; EdgeX Data Centers sold it to Tonaquint Data Centers in 2023, and Tonaquint was rebranded ValorC3 in 2025.
The entry is recorded as operating with no capacity, no acreage, no cost and no developer, sourced to a television report and a YouTube clip.
No power figure is published.
What is happening around it is larger.

A ten megawatt Cerebras Systems building sits 14 kilometres away, an Athlon Blockchain Technology site 34, and the Cloverleaf Project Open Sky proposal, at 1,400 megawatts, 37 kilometres off at Piedmont.
Oklahoma City adopted a data center moratorium on April 21, 2026, running to the end of the year, and three neighbouring places followed in June: Edmond, Luther and Norman.
None of those would reach a building already operating.
The nearest generators are the 126 megawatt Frontier plant five kilometres away, the 401 megawatt Mustang plant eight, the 487 megawatt McClain facility 14 and the 64 megawatt Tinker plant 21.
Pushback is recorded as unknown, and for a tornado-hardened box by the airport that is probably the truth.

unconfirmed: Everything found came from directory listings, the operator's own material and television coverage of the building's construction; the KFOR report in our record was not fetched and the second source is a YouTube clip that was not watched, so no source url is listed and each sentence is attributed to our record's source list. The build date is given as 2009 in one listing and 2010 in another. No power or water figure is published, and nothing is known about the building's tenants or its current load.

sentences.t: The county spent two and a half years vetting it without knowing whose it was.

On Wednesday, August 19, 2026 Google was confirmed as the end user of Project Clydesdale, a 506 acre data center campus in unincorporated Tulsa County west of Owasso, next to the Cherokee Industrial Park, developed by Beale Infrastructure, which broke ground in October 2025.

Cheyenne Morgan, who coordinates the Stop Data Colonialism Coalition, put the objection to the process rather than the building: "I don't believe that there was true community consent or engagement around this project."

County Commissioner Stan Sallee took it the other way: "The announcement today, very exciting, that it's Google ... to have Google announced as the end user is a tremendous boost to northeast Oklahoma."
Trystine Payfer, Google's public affairs manager for Oklahoma, said: "This project is far more than an infrastructure investment; it is a long-term commitment to Tulsa County's future."
The figures the company offered were about the state rather than the site.
Google said it had invested more than $15 billion in Oklahoma since 2011 and that its 2025 spending supported $2.6 billion of state economic activity.
The project includes about 1.5 miles of new water lines and an electrical training partnership aiming at more than 160 apprentices in Oklahoma by 2030.

Stacy Smith of the Tulsa Regional Chamber argued the benefit was wider than the direct jobs: "This isn't just a 100, 200 direct jobs. This is an ecosystem of activity and additional jobs that's going to follow."
The campus is recorded as under construction on 506 acres, with Beale Infrastructure and Google as developers, no capacity figure and no cost, and pushback now recorded as organised advocacy.
No megawatt figure has been published for a 506 acre Google campus.
An operating Cherokee data center sits one kilometre away, Meta's Tulsa campus under construction 15, and eight other sites within 30.
The nearest generators are the 330 megawatt Tulsa plant 19 kilometres off and the 1,342 megawatt Northeastern plant 26.

unconfirmed: A line attributed to Cheyenne Morgan, that "despite community pushback, Project Clydesdale got pushed forward anyways, without us knowing who the end user was", is not in the report read here; the words quoted above are hers instead. Stan Sallee's quotation is given there with a cut in the middle, and the clause the page had in that gap, about anticipating one of the top four companies, could not be confirmed. Google's reported gift of more than $2 million locally over two years is not in that report either and has come out. No megawatt or water figure has been published for the campus, beyond the 1.5 miles of new water lines. Our record marks pushback as unknown although the coalition quoted is organised against it, and the KJRH report on county residents' concerns was not fetched. The Tulsa Planning Commission submittal PDF in our record was not opened. What the two and a half year vetting process involved, and whether any of it was public, is not explained.

sentences.t: The car park filled before the meeting started.

On Monday, June 22, 2026 a crowd filled the council chamber at the Veterans' Event Center in Piedmont, in Canadian County, over Cloverleaf's proposed data center campus; the planning commission had recommended refusing the rezoning three weeks earlier, and the council ran out of time before the company's representatives, its chief executive among them, could present, so the decision went off to late July.

The figures Cloverleaf brought were up to 1.4 gigawatts of power, 75,000 gallons of water a day for up to four months in the initial phase with closed loop cooling, 60 decibels of noise, $9 million a year to the town in franchise fees and other payments, and up to 500 permanent jobs.
Aaron Bilyeu spoke for the company.
One resident summed up the objection: "Data centers are not making money. They are taking money."
Asked by the reporter whether anything Cloverleaf could say would change his mind, another answered: "No."
The objections were water, power and noise.
The project is recorded at 1,400 megawatts on 633 acres, proposed, costing $1 billion, with Cloverleaf Infrastructure as developer, at medium confidence, and resistance marked as organised advocacy.
Cloverleaf is the same company whose Dundee proposal in Michigan collapsed in October 2025 after the village shelved its pre-agreement.
The scale is the thing.

The nearest generators are the 298 megawatt Kingfisher wind farm six kilometres away, the 294 megawatt Spring Creek gas plant 12, the 294 megawatt Canadian Hills wind farm 24 and the 401 megawatt Mustang plant 30.
Those four together make about 1.3 gigawatts, slightly less than this one campus would draw.
Canadian County has no moratorium on record; the nearest are Oklahoma City's from April 21, 2026 and Edmond's from June 8.

unconfirmed: No resident or council member is named in the report read here, only the company's representative Aaron Bilyeu. The acreage and cost in our record are not confirmed by it. The water figure of 75,000 gallons a day is described as applying to an initial phase for up to four months, which does not tell a reader what the campus would use once running, and no full-build figure was given. The Data Center Dynamics report in our record is not fetchable, and the company's own FAQ page and the residents' Facebook group were not opened. What the council decided in late July 2026 is unknown.

sentences.t: Somebody sent the city fake emails supporting this one.

Beale Infrastructure proposed the Project Atlas data center on 270 acres at 16192 State Highway 51B near Coweta, in Wagoner County, in at least one phase with three more possible, each of about 200,000 square feet.
In late March 2026 the planning commission voted 4 to 1 to recommend refusing the rezoning, and the company withdrew.
Residents had objected to local officials signing nondisclosure agreements and to the water and energy the campus would use.
A Facebook group formed against it, and a change.org petition asked that the data center be kept out of Coweta.
A local television station separately reported on fake emails of support sent to the city, under the headline "Data center scandal: who sent fake emails of support for Project Atlas?".

Beale Infrastructure said: "While we have made the decision to withdraw our data center project in Coweta, known locally as Project Atlas, we look forward to continuing to build meaningful community investments in other locations in Oklahoma."
It has: the company is behind Google's Project Clydesdale at Owasso, 30 kilometres away and under construction, and Project Mustang at Claremore, which Claremore approved.
The project is recorded as cancelled with no acreage, no capacity and no cost, and Beale Infrastructure as developer.
It also records a ban on data centers on Cherokee Nation tribal lands, with no date attached, alongside the Tulsa and Broken Arrow moratoriums.
The 1,086 megawatt Oneta Energy Center is 15 kilometres away, the 1,510 megawatt Muskogee plant 32 and the 1,070 megawatt Riverside plant 33.
CoreWeave's Muskogee site is under construction 24 kilometres off.

unconfirmed: All three Data Center Dynamics reports in our record are not fetchable, and the KTUL, KOSU, News on 6 and KRMG accounts were found only in search summaries, so no source url is listed and each sentence is attributed to our record's source list. No resident, planning commissioner or city official is quoted. The fake emails story is referred to by headline only; who sent them, and what came of it, is unestablished. Our record's address gives 6192 State Highway 51B while the reporting gives 16192. No megawatt or water figure was ever published. The Cherokee Nation ban in our record has no date and could not be verified.
